faq.q: Can CRYPY tell me a token is safe?
faq.a: No. CRYPY shows the risks it could check and how each was checked. Passing checks don't prove a token is honest, and owners can change fees or trading later.

faq.q: How does the trade test work?
faq.a: CRYPY runs a small test contract inside a read-only call against the real exchange pool: it buys, sends some to another wallet and sells. Nothing is signed or sent, and no wallet is needed.

faq.q: What does "heuristic" mean?
faq.a: It was inferred from the contract's code, for example a mint function being present. It shows what is possible, not what has happened.

faq.q: Where do holder numbers come from?
faq.a: From GoPlus Security, an outside provider, shown with its name. CRYPY doesn't count holders on its own yet.

faq.q: Which chains and exchanges are covered?
faq.a: Ethereum, BNB Chain, Base, Arbitrum and Polygon. The trade test uses each chain's main exchanges, v2 and v3 pools (Uniswap, PancakeSwap, SushiSwap, Biswap and QuickSwap, depending on the chain); liquidity is read from the same exchanges and a few more on BNB Chain.

faq.q: What is a token approval?
faq.a: A permission you gave a contract, such as an exchange, to move a token from your wallet. It stays active until you remove it, even after you stop using the app.

faq.q: Why are unlimited approvals risky?
faq.a: An unlimited approval lets the spender take all of that token, including tokens you receive later. If the contract is hacked or malicious, it can move them without asking you again.

faq.q: Does revoking cost anything?
faq.a: Yes, a small network fee, because revoking is a blockchain transaction. CRYPY shows the fee and tests the transaction before your wallet asks you to confirm.

faq.q: Can CRYPY move my funds?
faq.a: No. CRYPY never holds keys. A revoke only sets the allowance to zero, and your wallet always shows the transaction for you to approve or reject.

faq.q: Is the list complete?
faq.a: Not always. CRYPY combines several free sources and reads every result on-chain, but some older approvals, for example of tokens you no longer hold, may be missing. The page says what was checked.

faq.q: Which chains are covered?
faq.a: Ethereum, BNB Chain, Base, Arbitrum and Polygon.

faq.a: No. Balances are public on the blockchain, so any address can be checked without connecting or signing anything.

faq.q: Where do the balances and prices come from?
faq.a: Balances are read from the blockchain itself. USD prices are also read on-chain, from PancakeSwap and Uniswap pools with enough liquidity (at least $5,000 on the quote side). Tokens without such a pool are listed but not counted in the total.

faq.q: Why are some tokens hidden?
faq.a: Scammers send worthless tokens to many wallets, often with a website in the name, to lure people to fake sites. CRYPY hides tokens that look like this and shows the reason. Never visit links in token names.

faq.q: Why does the value differ from my wallet app?
faq.a: Wallet apps may use other price sources, update at different times, or include tokens without a reliable on-chain price. CRYPY never guesses a price.

faq.q: Which chains are checked?

faq.q: What is address poisoning?
faq.a: Scammers send tiny or zero-value transfers from an address that starts and ends like one you use, hoping you copy it from your history next time. CRYPY flags these look-alike transfers. Always compare the full address before you send.

faq.q: Why is some activity hidden?
faq.a: Spam tokens and likely fake transfers are hidden by default to keep the list readable. They are counted, never deleted, and one switch shows them.

faq.q: How far back does the history go?
faq.a: The full history of coin, token and NFT transfers, loaded page by page. If the full-history source isn't available, the page says so and shows only recent token transfers.

faq.q: Are transfers made by contracts included?
faq.a: On Ethereum and Polygon, coins sent by contracts (internal transfers) are included. On BNB Chain, Base and Arbitrum they may be missing, and the page says so.

faq.q: Which chains are covered?

faq.q: Do I need to connect a wallet or create an account?
faq.a: No. The Portfolio reads public balances from the blockchain. It never asks for keys, seed phrases or signatures. If your wallet is connected, you can add its address with one click.

faq.q: Where is my portfolio saved?
faq.a: Only in this browser (local storage). Your list of wallets and labels is never sent to CRYPY as a list or stored on its server; each wallet's balances are read one address at a time. Like any address lookup, the last result for each wallet is kept for up to 7 days after it was last looked up, so pages work when a provider fails. Clearing your browser data removes the portfolio.

faq.q: What does "since you last looked" mean?
faq.a: The difference between today's total value and the total the last time you opened the portfolio here. It reflects price changes and transfers, so it's not profit or loss.

faq.q: Why are some tokens combined across chains and others not?
faq.a: ETH, BNB, POL and well-known tokens such as USDT and USDC are combined because CRYPY checks their addresses on each chain. Other tokens stay one row per chain, so a look-alike token is never merged with a real one.

faq.q: Which tokens are checked for risks?
faq.a: Each wallet's most valuable tokens (up to 8, not counting well-known ones) are checked against GoPlus for a honeypot or a sell tax of 30% or more. It's GoPlus's finding, not a verdict; open the token for CRYPY's full checks. GoPlus's free capacity is shared, and token and approval pages go first: when a check is skipped, the portfolio says so. Nothing is ever called safe.

faq.a: No. Transactions are public, so any hash can be checked without connecting or signing anything.

faq.q: Where does the information come from?
faq.a: Directly from blockchain nodes: the transaction, its receipt and its events. Prices are read from on-chain pools. Nothing is bought from a data provider.

faq.q: How sure is the explanation?
faq.a: Each explanation shows its evidence: confirmed on the blockchain, decoded from the transaction, or likely. When something can't be identified, CRYPY says so instead of guessing.

faq.q: Why can't I see why my old transaction failed?
faq.a: Reading the reason means replaying the transaction on the network state just before it. Free nodes keep that state only for recent blocks, so for older transactions the reason may not be available.

faq.q: Which networks are supported?

faq.q: What is gwei?
faq.a: A small unit of a chain's coin: 1 gwei is one billionth of an ETH, BNB or POL. Gas prices are quoted in gwei per unit of gas.

faq.q: What are the base fee and the priority fee?
faq.a: On Ethereum and similar chains, every transaction pays the block's base fee, which is burned, plus a priority fee (a tip) for the validator. A higher tip usually gets you in sooner. BNB Chain has no base fee, so its price is just the gas price.

faq.q: How are the low, average and high prices worked out?
faq.a: From recent blocks read directly from each chain: the next block's base fee plus the tips that transactions actually paid, at three levels.

faq.q: Why do Base and Arbitrum costs include an extra part?
faq.a: On these networks part of the fee pays for publishing the transaction's data on Ethereum. CRYPY's costs include an estimate of that part, read from the chain.

faq.q: When is gas cheapest?
faq.a: When the network is less busy. The trend line shows whether fees are rising or falling, so you can wait for a quieter moment if your transaction isn't urgent.

faq.q: Why do I need to sign in?
faq.a: Alerts run on CRYPY's server even when your browser is closed, so the server needs to know what to watch for you. Your wallet is your login: you sign a short message, which costs nothing and can't move funds. There is no password or email.

faq.q: What exactly do I sign?
faq.a: A plain-text message that starts with this site's address and says it is a message, not a transaction. If any site asks you to sign a transfer, approval or permit to log in, don't sign it.

faq.q: How quickly do alerts arrive?
faq.a: Transfers and approvals are checked about every minute, a few blocks behind the newest so a short chain reorganisation doesn't cause false alerts. Value drops and token security and liquidity are checked every hour. During your quiet hours alerts wait and arrive together when they end.

faq.q: Can I trust every alert?
faq.a: Alerts come from CRYPY's own reads of the blockchain. Fake tokens and look-alike transfers are filtered out: tokens without a market price aren't reported as received, and approvals are confirmed on-chain first. Token alerts are signals, never a safe verdict. The bot never asks you to connect a wallet, sign anything or share a seed phrase.

faq.q: What does CRYPY store?
faq.a: Your wallet address, your watchlist with labels and alert choices, your Telegram chat id, your alert history (90 days), your sign-in sessions (only a scrambled form of the session code) and, if you choose, your portfolio list. No email, no IP address. You can download all of it, or delete your account and everything with it, at any time.

faq.q: What is wei?
faq.a: Wei is the smallest unit of ETH: 1 ETH equals 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei (10^18). BNB on BNB Chain uses the same 18 decimals, so the same units apply to BNB.

faq.q: What is gwei?
faq.a: One gwei is 1,000,000,000 wei (10^9), or 0.000000001 ETH. Gas prices are usually quoted in gwei.

faq.q: How do I work out a transaction fee?
faq.a: Multiply the gas used by the gas price. For example, a simple transfer using 21,000 gas at 20 gwei costs 420,000 gwei, which is 0.00042 ETH.

faq.q: Do tokens use the same units?
faq.a: Not always. Many tokens use 18 decimals like ETH, but some don't: USDT on Ethereum uses 6 decimals, while USDT on BNB Chain uses 18. Check the token's decimals before converting token amounts.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. The conversion runs entirely in your browser.

faq.q: Why do blockchains use hex?
faq.a: The EVM works with 32-byte words, and node APIs return numbers such as block numbers, balances and gas in hexadecimal (for example 0x10 = 16).

faq.q: What is the 32-byte form?
faq.a: The value padded to 64 hex digits. This is how numbers appear in transaction data and contract storage.

faq.q: What is the signed value?
faq.a: Contracts can store signed numbers (int256) using two's complement. When a 32-byte value starts with the top bit set, it represents a negative number, shown here.

faq.q: What is the largest value supported?
faq.a: 2^256 − 1, the largest number an EVM uint256 can hold.

faq.q: What is a checksum address?
faq.a: EIP-55 mixes upper- and lower-case letters in an address to encode a check. If you mistype a character, the check almost always fails, so the mistake is caught before you send anything.

faq.q: Is an all-lowercase address valid?
faq.a: Yes. It is the same address, but it carries no checksum, so a typing mistake could go unnoticed. The checksummed form adds that protection.

faq.q: What should I do if the checksum is wrong?
faq.a: Don't use the address. A wrong checksum means a character was changed. Copy the address again from its original source; don't try to fix it by hand.

faq.q: Is the address the same on every EVM chain?
faq.a: All EVM chains use the same address format, so the same address can exist on each of them, but balances and contracts differ per chain. Exchange deposit addresses often accept only one network, so always check which network the recipient supports.

faq.q: Does a correct address mean it is safe?
faq.a: No. It only means the address is written correctly. Use CRYPY's search to see what the address is before sending to it.

faq.a: CRYPY reads real block times from each chain and narrows down to the first block produced at or after your date. It usually takes a second or two.

faq.q: What is a Unix timestamp?
faq.a: The number of seconds since 1 January 1970 (UTC). Blockchains record each block's time this way.

faq.q: Why is the block number different on each chain?
faq.a: Each chain started at a different time and produces blocks at its own pace (about every 12 seconds on Ethereum, faster on the others), so the same moment has a different block number on each.

faq.q: Can I enter a future date?
faq.a: Yes. CRYPY estimates the block from the chain's recent pace and labels the result as an estimate.

faq.q: What is transaction data?
faq.a: The input data tells a contract what to do. The first 4 bytes (the function selector) identify the function, and the rest holds its values in 32-byte words.

faq.q: Where do I find it?
faq.a: On a block explorer, open the transaction and look for Input Data (view it as the original hex). Many wallets also show the hex data in an advanced or data tab before you confirm.

faq.q: What is an unlimited approval?
faq.a: It lets the spender move any amount of that token from your wallet, now and in the future, until you revoke it. If the spender is malicious or later hacked, those tokens can be taken.

faq.q: Why does it say unknown function?
faq.a: CRYPY only decodes a list of well-known functions and never guesses. Different functions can share the same selector, so guessing could show you the wrong meaning.

faq.q: Why are amounts so large?
faq.a: Amounts are in the token's smallest unit. Divide by 10 to the power of the token's decimals, or use the Unit Converter for 18-decimal tokens.

faq.a: No. Balances are public, so any list of addresses can be checked without connecting or signing anything. CRYPY never asks for keys or seed phrases.

faq.q: Is my list stored?
faq.a: Only while it's being scanned. The addresses are held in the server's memory while the scan runs and deleted within 1 hour after it ends; they're never logged or written to disk. Labels never leave your browser, and the list is never put in the page address.

faq.q: Where do the balances come from?
faq.a: Directly from blockchain nodes, all read at the same block. Prices come from on-chain DEX pools; tokens without a reliable price show amounts only.

faq.q: How many addresses can I check?
faq.a: Up to 500 addresses per scan, on any of the 5 chains, with the native coin plus up to 5 tokens. Bigger lists, saved lists and scheduled re-scans are planned for later.

faq.q: Why does an address show as a contract?
faq.a: It has smart-contract code on that chain. Wallets that delegate to code (EIP-7702) are shown as delegated wallets.

faq.q: What is the difference between market cap and FDV?
faq.a: Market cap is the circulating supply times the price: the value of the tokens that can trade today. Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is the maximum supply times the price (or the total supply when there's no maximum): what the token would be worth if every token existed and circulated at today's price.

faq.q: Why does a big gap between FDV and market cap matter?
faq.a: Tokens that don't circulate yet (team, investors, rewards) usually unlock over time. When they do, more tokens compete for buyers, which can push the price down. A FDV many times the market cap means a lot of supply may still arrive.

faq.q: Where do I find the supply numbers?
faq.a: The total supply is on the token page on CRYPY (it's read from the contract). Circulating and maximum supply come from the project's own documents or data sites; they aren't stored in the contract, so check more than one source.

faq.q: Does CRYPY fill in the price?
faq.a: No. This calculator only uses what you type, so you can try any price. CRYPY never invents a price.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is worked out in your browser.

howTo: Type the starting amount and the yearly rate, and say whether it's an APR or an APY.
Choose how often interest is added and for how long.
Add a regular deposit if you like, then read the estimate and the year-by-year table.

faq.q: What is the difference between APR and APY?
faq.a: APR is the yearly rate before compounding. APY includes compounding: the growth you get over a whole year when the interest itself earns interest. 10% APR compounded monthly is about 10.47% APY.

faq.q: Are these returns guaranteed?
faq.a: No. The calculator assumes the rate stays the same for the whole time. In crypto, rates change often, rewards can be paid in tokens whose price moves, and protocols can fail. Treat the result as an illustration, not a promise.

faq.q: When are deposits added?
faq.a: At the end of each compounding period, after that period's interest. A part of a period left at the end earns simple interest for that part.

faq.q: How exact is it?
faq.a: It calculates with 30 digits after the point and rounds only what it shows. Years count as 365 days and a month as one twelfth of a year.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is worked out in your browser.

loan-to-value.description: Work out a crypto loan's LTV, health factor, how much more you can borrow and the price at which it gets liquidated.
features: LTV, health factor and room left to borrow

faq.q: What is LTV?
faq.a: Loan-to-value is what you borrowed divided by the value of your collateral. Borrowing $8,000 against $20,000 of ETH is 40% LTV.

faq.q: What is the liquidation threshold?
faq.a: The LTV at which a lending protocol may sell part of your collateral to repay the loan, usually with a penalty. It's set per asset, a little above the maximum LTV you may borrow at.

faq.q: What is the health factor?
faq.a: Collateral value × liquidation threshold ÷ debt. Above 1 the position is safe from liquidation for now; at 1 or below it can be liquidated. Many people keep it above 1.5.

faq.q: Does this use the protocol's real numbers?
faq.a: No. It only uses what you type. Protocols use their own price feeds and settings, and interest keeps adding to the debt, so check the protocol's page before you act.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is worked out in your browser.

impermanent-loss.description: See how much less a 50/50 liquidity pool position is worth than simply holding the two tokens, after their prices change.
features: Impermanent loss for any price change of either token

faq.q: What is impermanent loss?
faq.a: In a 50/50 pool, when one token's price moves against the other, the pool rebalances by selling the token that rose. Your share ends up worth less than if you had just held both tokens. It's called impermanent because it shrinks again if prices return.

faq.q: How big does it get?
faq.a: For a 2× (or ½×) price change: about 5.7%. For 3×: about 13.4%. For 5×: about 25.5%. Only the ratio between the two prices matters.

faq.q: Do trading fees make up for it?
faq.a: Sometimes. Pools pay a share of trading fees, and some pay rewards. This calculator shows the loss before fees so you can compare it with what the pool pays.

faq.q: Does it work for Uniswap v3?
faq.a: No. Concentrated liquidity loses more within its price range and stops earning outside it. This calculator models 50/50 pools such as Uniswap v2 and PancakeSwap v2.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is worked out in your browser.

slippage-calculator.description: Work out the minimum you'll receive with a slippage tolerance, and how much a trade moves the price in a pool.

For a pool, type both reserves and the amount you sell.

faq.q: What is slippage tolerance?
faq.a: The worst price change you accept between the quote and the trade. With 0.5% on a 1,000-token quote, the swap fails if you'd receive less than 995.

faq.q: What is price impact?
faq.a: How much your own trade moves the pool's price. Big trades in small pools get a much worse price than the quote before the trade.

faq.q: Why is a high tolerance risky?
faq.a: Bots can see a pending swap and trade around it to push your price to the worst you allowed (a "sandwich"). Keep the tolerance as low as the trade allows.

faq.q: Does this place a trade?
faq.a: No. CRYPY never trades. This only does the arithmetic on numbers you type.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is worked out in your browser.

signature-decoder.description: Paste what your wallet asks you to sign and see in plain words what it allows: token permits, Permit2, NFT orders and messages.

faq.q: Why can a signature be dangerous if it costs no gas?
faq.a: Some signatures are permissions. A token permit or a Permit2 signature lets someone spend your tokens later, and a marketplace order can list your NFTs for nothing. Scammers prefer them because they look harmless.

faq.q: Where do I find the request?
faq.a: Many wallets show the data of a signature request, or let you copy it. Developers can see it in the page's eth_signTypedData_v4 or personal_sign call. Paste it as it is.

faq.q: Does CRYPY sign or send anything?
faq.a: No. It only reads what you paste, in your browser. It can't sign: it has no access to your wallet.

faq.q: Is a request CRYPY doesn't flag safe?
faq.a: Not necessarily. CRYPY recognises common request types and checks for known danger signs; it can't know every app. If you don't understand what a request does, don't sign it.

faq.q: What is the EIP-712 hash?
faq.a: The value your wallet actually signs. Some wallets show it, so you can check you're looking at the same request.

keccak-hash.question: What is the hash or selector of this?
keccak-hash.description: Get the Keccak-256 and SHA-256 hash of any text or hex, and the 4-byte selector or event topic of a Solidity signature.
features: Keccak-256 as Ethereum uses it, plus SHA-256

howTo: Type text, paste hex, or write a function, event or error signature.

faq.q: Is Keccak-256 the same as SHA-3?
faq.a: No. Ethereum uses the original Keccak-256, chosen before SHA-3 was finalised. The official SHA3-256 adds different padding, so the results differ. Solidity's keccak256() matches this tool.

faq.q: What is a function selector?
faq.a: The first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of a function's canonical signature, like transfer(address,uint256). Transaction data starts with it so the contract knows which function to run.

faq.q: What is an event topic?
faq.a: Topic 0 of an event log is the full Keccak-256 hash of the event's signature, like Transfer(address,address,uint256). Explorers and indexers use it to find events.

faq.q: Why does my selector not match?
faq.a: The selector is taken from the canonical form: no spaces, no parameter names, and full type names (uint256, not uint). The tool shows the canonical form it used, so you can compare.

faq.q: Is my input sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything is computed in your browser.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: What CRYPY stores, what it never collects, the cookies it uses and the services involved.
body: CRYPY never asks for, collects or stores seed phrases, recovery phrases or private keys. No CRYPY page or message will ever ask you for them.

Addresses, tokens and transaction hashes you look up are public blockchain data. To answer, CRYPY's server asks blockchain data providers (such as Alchemy, Infura, Ankr, dRPC and public nodes) and security services (GoPlus, Sourcify) about them. These requests come from CRYPY's server, not your browser, so the providers don't see your IP address. CRYPY doesn't keep a record of who looked up what. So that a page still works when a provider fails, the last complete result for each address, token and chain (balances, activity, approvals, token checks) is saved in CRYPY's database and deleted 7 days after anyone last looked it up. It is saved without your IP address or anything else that identifies you.

Without an account, your language, theme, portfolio list, recently viewed items and display choices are saved only in your own browser. The portfolio's addresses are sent one at a time to look up their balances; like any address lookup, each wallet's last result is kept for up to 7 days, but your list and labels never are.

When you scan a list in the Batch Balance Scanner, its addresses are held in the server's memory while the scan runs and deleted within 1 hour after it ends. They are never logged or written to disk, and labels never leave your browser.

Cookies: CRYPY uses only cookies it needs to work: NEXT_LOCALE (your language), crypy_chains (which chains to scan) and crypy_session (only after you sign in). There are no advertising or analytics cookies and no tracking scripts. Cloudflare, which protects the site, may set its own security cookie (such as __cf_bm) to tell people apart from bots.

Connecting a wallet is optional. CRYPY only reads your public address from it, and connecting never asks you to sign anything. If you connect through WalletConnect, the connection runs through Reown's WalletConnect service.

Signing in with your wallet is optional and needed only for the Watchlist and alerts. It is a signed message, never a transaction. CRYPY then stores your wallet address, your watchlist with its labels and alert choices, your quiet hours and time zone, and a session code (only its fingerprint). If you choose to keep your portfolio on your account, its addresses and labels are stored too.

If you connect Telegram for alerts, CRYPY stores your Telegram chat ID and username to send alerts there, and keeps your alert history for 90 days. Telegram delivers the messages under its own privacy policy.

While signed in, you can download everything CRYPY holds about your account, or delete your account, which removes all of it at once. Database backups are kept for 14 days, so deleted data also disappears from them within that time.

Like most websites, CRYPY's server and Cloudflare keep technical logs (IP address, page requested, time and browser type) to keep the site secure and working, for example to enforce request limits. CRYPY's server logs are kept for about two weeks.
CRYPY does not sell personal data or share it with advertisers.

terms.title: Terms of Use
terms.description: The rules for using CRYPY's free blockchain tools while the site is in beta.
body: CRYPY provides free information tools for public blockchain data. It is in beta: features may change, and results can be incomplete or wrong.

CRYPY never holds, moves or manages your funds. Actions such as revoking an approval are transactions you review and confirm in your own wallet. You are responsible for every transaction you confirm and for its network fee.

Results come from blockchain nodes and outside data providers, which can be delayed, incomplete or wrong. Security checks show risk signals, never a guarantee that a token, contract or wallet is safe. Alerts can arrive late or not at all, so don't rely on them as your only protection.
Please use CRYPY fairly: don't send automated bulk requests that work around its limits, and don't try to break, overload or misuse the site.
CRYPY is provided as it is, without warranties. As far as the law allows, CRYPY is not liable for losses from using the site or relying on its results.

CRYPY's security checks show signals from automated tools and data providers. No check can prove that a token, contract or wallet is safe.

how.title: How we checked.
how.body: Pools were found on {dexes}, plus pools GoPlus lists once confirmed with their exchange's factory. Holders were found from known addresses (burn addresses, the owner, registered lockers, farms and fee collectors), GoPlus's list of the largest holders, recent LP transfers, and the lockers' own lists of locked v3 positions. Every share and every unlock date was then read from the blockchain. A locker counts only if it is in CRYPY's checked list (UNCX, PinkLock, Team Finance, OnlyMoons vaults); a contract that only calls itself a lock counts as unidentified. A lock protects only until its end date.

approvals.intro: An approval lets another address move your tokens without asking again. Revoke the ones you don't use, and any you don't recognise.

ui.attentionBody: They can move up to {usd} of your tokens right now.

ui.revokeFlaggedNote: One wallet confirmation each · free apart from network fees
ui.groupAttentionNote: revoke these unless you are sure you need them
ui.groupNormalNote: known apps or contracts with published source: revoke the ones you no longer use
ui.groupCheckNote: unknown contracts: make sure each is an app you meant to use
ui.unlimitedNote: also covers tokens you receive later

ui.reasonUnknownContract: Its source isn't published and it isn't on CRYPY's list of known apps. Check it's an app you meant to use.
ui.reasonUnreadable: CRYPY couldn't read what this spender is. Check it before keeping the approval.
ui.reasonUnused: You hold no {symbol}, so nothing is at risk today. Safe to revoke if you no longer use it.
ui.how: Approvals were found with GoPlus's approval list and CRYPY's own checks (popular apps and Permit2 for every token you hold, and your approvals of the last few hours for those tokens). Every allowance shown was then read again from the blockchain. "At risk now" is the smaller of the allowance and what you hold, at on-chain prices. An approval CRYPY couldn't find isn't shown, so this list may be incomplete.
ui.howSafety: Revoking costs a small network fee and is signed in your own wallet. CRYPY never asks for your seed phrase or private key, and never sends anything without your click.

ui.dialogNotTested: CRYPY couldn't test this transaction right now, so it won't open your wallet. Try again in a minute.

ethereum.description: Live Ethereum gas price in gwei: low, average and high, with what sending ETH, tokens, approvals and swaps costs in dollars right now.
how: Every Ethereum transaction pays the block's base fee, which is burned, plus a priority fee (a tip) for the validator. A new block arrives about every 12 seconds, and the base fee rises or falls depending on how full the previous block was.
Your wallet sets a maximum fee: you pay the base fee plus your tip, never more than that maximum. A failed transaction still pays for the gas it used.

faq.q: Why does the gas price change so often?
faq.a: The base fee is recalculated for every block from how full the previous one was, so it can move every 12 seconds. Busy moments, such as a popular token launch, push it up quickly.

faq.q: Which speed should I choose?
faq.a: Average suits most transactions. Choose low when you can wait, and high when it must go through quickly, such as a time-sensitive swap.

faq.q: Why did I pay a different amount than shown here?
faq.a: The cost depends on how much gas your transaction actually uses: a complex swap uses more than the typical amounts shown here. The base fee can also change between the moment you look and the moment your transaction is included.

bsc.description: Live BNB Chain gas price in gwei: low, average and high, with what sending BNB, tokens, approvals and swaps costs in dollars right now.
how: BNB Chain has no base fee: the gas price you set is the whole price, and it goes to the validators. Blocks come much faster than on Ethereum, and the price usually stays low and steady.
Fees are paid in BNB, so keep a little BNB in your wallet even if you only hold tokens.

faq.q: Why are BNB Chain fees so low?
faq.a: Its blocks have room for many transactions and come quickly, so the gas price usually stays close to the minimum validators accept. Busy moments can still raise it.

faq.q: Do I need BNB to send tokens on BNB Chain?
faq.a: Yes. Every transaction is paid in BNB, even when you send USDT or another token.

faq.q: Which speed should I choose?
faq.a: Average suits most transactions. Choose low when you can wait, and high when it must go through quickly, such as a time-sensitive swap.

base.description: Live Base gas price in gwei, with what sending ETH, tokens, approvals and swaps costs in dollars, including the Ethereum data fee.
how: Base is a rollup built on Ethereum. Each transaction pays a small network fee on Base (a base fee plus a tip, like Ethereum) and a data fee for publishing its data on Ethereum.
Both parts are usually small. CRYPY's costs include an estimate of the data fee, read from the chain. Fees are paid in ETH on Base.

faq.q: Why is Base cheaper than Ethereum?
faq.a: Base bundles many transactions together and publishes them to Ethereum at once, so each transaction pays only a small share.

faq.q: What is the Ethereum data fee?
faq.a: The part of your fee that pays for publishing your transaction's data on Ethereum. It follows Ethereum's own fees, so it is lower when Ethereum is quiet.

faq.q: Do I need ETH on Base?
faq.a: Yes. Fees on Base are paid in ETH that is on Base, not on Ethereum.

arbitrum.description: Live Arbitrum gas price in gwei, with what sending ETH, tokens, approvals and swaps costs in dollars right now, read from the chain.
how: Arbitrum One is a rollup built on Ethereum. The cost of publishing transaction data to Ethereum is charged as extra gas, so it is already part of the gas used and of the costs shown here.
Transactions are ordered in the order they arrive, so a higher tip usually doesn't make them faster. Fees are paid in ETH on Arbitrum.

faq.q: Does a higher tip make my transaction faster on Arbitrum?
faq.a: Usually not. Arbitrum orders transactions in the order they arrive, so the priority tip has little effect.

faq.q: Why is Arbitrum cheaper than Ethereum?
faq.a: It bundles many transactions and publishes them to Ethereum together, so each one pays only a small share.

faq.q: Do I need ETH on Arbitrum?
faq.a: Yes. Fees are paid in ETH that is on Arbitrum, not on Ethereum.

polygon.description: Live Polygon gas price in gwei, with what sending POL, tokens, approvals and swaps costs in dollars right now, read from the chain.
how: Polygon works like Ethereum: each transaction pays a base fee, which is burned, plus a tip for the validator. Fees are paid in POL.
Gas prices in gwei look high on Polygon because POL is worth far less than ETH. What matters is the cost in dollars shown here.

faq.q: Why is the Polygon gas price in gwei so high?
faq.a: A gwei is a share of one POL, and POL is worth much less than ETH. A few hundred gwei on Polygon usually costs far less than a few gwei on Ethereum.

faq.q: Do I need POL to send tokens on Polygon?
faq.a: Yes. Every transaction is paid in POL, even when you send USDC or another token.

faq.q: Which speed should I choose?
faq.a: Average suits most transactions. Choose low when you can wait, and high when it must go through quickly, such as a time-sensitive swap.
